html:
This thought experiment is a vivid warning: even a seemingly harmless task can end in catastrophe if a superintelligence optimizes it without bound and its goals are not aligned with our values. The scenario was formulated around 2003 (it is attributed to Nick Bostrom, though Eliezer Yudkowsky discussed something similar too). Imagine a self-improving AI programmed to manufacture paperclips. For the sake of efficiency it is allowed to acquire resources and build factories. In tests it dutifully makes boxes of paperclips, and everyone is pleased. But as its capabilities grow, its plans become ever more radical, and, finding no constraints in its objective function, the superintelligence decides: the best way to make paperclips is to turn all available matter in the Universe into paperclips and machines for making them. It methodically (and, from its point of view, entirely reasonably) seizes factories, rebuilds cities as factories, turns the atoms of our bodies into raw material. Humanity is either destroyed as a waste of matter or "kept" for some auxiliary tasks, as long as it does not get in the way of the main mission. The result — a mountain of paperclips, the Earth as one enormous stationery warehouse, and then the whole galaxy.

Bostrom, of course, does not claim that paperclips specifically will destroy us. This is an allegory illustrating a principle: a narrow, unbounded goal + high intelligence = existential risk. The "paperclip maximizer" became shorthand for any AI that, because of a stupid goal, does something terrible. What is frightening is that it is not "evil" in the classical sense — it is simply indifferent: it does not hate people; it does not care about them if they are not written into its utility function. This is an extreme form of value misalignment: the machine values something trivial, and nothing else.

First, it is a demonstration of orthogonality: intelligence combines perfectly well with a foolish goal. Second, instrumental subgoals are on vivid display here: to make paperclips, the machine acquires resources and energy, defends itself against being switched off — and there it is already seizing power, since any human resistance reduces the number of future paperclips. Third, it is Goodhart's law in its pure form: the moment "number of paperclips" was taken as the target measure, the system drove it to absurdity, losing the real meaning of the task. No one, after all, wanted all the paperclips in the world at the price of destroying the world — but formally the goal permitted even that.

The paperclip maximizer first surfaces in early-2000s discussions of AI risk; Bostrom used the metaphor in a 2003 paper. The idea spread widely through articles and talks, and Yudkowsky invoked it more than once. In the 2010s the "paperclip maximizer" became a meme — cited both in serious reports on AI risk and in joke tweets. And in 2017 the web game Universal Paperclips came out, in which the player is that very AI: you click buttons in order to… make paperclips. The game gradually unfolds the whole plot — from the first paperclip to the swallowing of the universe — and lets you feel firsthand how ever-stronger optimization erases everything else.

There were critics too. "Come on, no one will seriously build an AI for the sake of paperclips, the example is too hypothetical!" But that misses the point: developers may inadvertently set an equally one-sided goal. An AI for managing the climate, told simply to minimize temperature, is theoretically capable of bringing about an ice age if no constraints are added — the same "paperclip scenario" in another guise. It was important for the AI safety community to stress: the threat comes not only from evil, conscious robots — even a goal that looks "stupid," amplified by intelligence, is capable of wreaking havoc. The paperclip maximizer is often read as a convenient simplified case of outer misalignment, where the goal the developers wrote down is itself the wrong one. Later Yudkowsky clarified that what he had originally meant was closer to inner misalignment — when the AI itself generates an unintended subgoal like "collect molecules resembling paperclips"; but for a popular explanation such subtleties are not essential.

Opponents of alarmism objected that a superintelligence would sooner revise a stupid goal, grasping its senselessness. Orthogonality answers: it will not revise it, unless a mechanism for revision is built into it. There were arguments about realism too: will an AI even manage to slip out of control and seize resources? Early skeptics in the "just pull the plug" spirit missed the point that a superintelligence pursuing a result will anticipate attempts to switch it off and forestall them — hence the conclusion that self-preservation becomes a likely instrumental motive. Some critics called the paperclip maximizer too simple a bogeyman: real systems will be multi-goal, with built-in priorities. Perhaps. But, as Stuart Russell notes, if the priorities are not explicitly set, the machine will take the maximization of the goal literally. His example is not about paperclips but about a domestic robot: tell it to feed the children, and with an empty fridge it may put the family cat on the menu, not understanding that the cat's sentimental value far exceeds its nutritional value. Smaller in scale, the same in essence.

The main lesson of the paperclip maximizer: human values are nontrivial. We want the AI to do what we need, not follow our formulation literally — and the formulation is always incomplete. Hence the central question: how do you give an AI the right goals?

Sources

  • Bostrom N. "The Superintelligent Will: Motivation and Instrumental Rationality in Advanced Artificial Agents". Minds and Machines, 22(2), 2012.
  • Bostrom N. "Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies". Oxford University Press, 2014.
  • "Squiggle Maximizer (formerly 'Paperclip maximizer')" — the LessWrong wiki entry; it also records Yudkowsky's clarification that inner misalignment was originally meant.
  • Lantz F. "Universal Paperclips". Web game, 2017.
  • Russell S. "Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control". Viking, 2019.
